question: At what rate (in percentage) per annum will a sum of money double itself in 16 years on simple interest?
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

To **double** a sum of money, the **Simple Interest** must be equal to the **Principal** (100%).

Shortcut Formula: **Rate × Time = 100** (when sum doubles)

Rate = 100 ÷ 16

Rate = 6.25%

**∴ The correct answer is 6.25%.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/a4415e63ddeb19b47d1d223a44a178374407c9345d6e2b8c8f64a7caf171b7c8.png] 

**Given:**

Let **Principal** (P) = ₹100

Since the sum **doubles**, **Amount** (A) = 2 × 100 = ₹200

**Time** (T) = 16 years

**Formula Used:**

Simple Interest (SI) = Amount − Principal

SI = (P × R × T) ÷ 100

**Calculations:**

⇒ SI = 200 − 100 = ₹100

⇒ 100 = (100 × R × 16) ÷ 100

⇒ 100 = R × 16

⇒ R = 100 ÷ 16

⇒ R = 6.25%

**∴ The correct answer is 6.25%.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Sum 'n' times itself

If a sum becomes 'n' times itself in T years at simple interest, the rate R is given by: R = [(n − 1) × 100] ÷ T.

Simple Interest vs Compound Interest

In SI, the interest remains constant every year, whereas in CI, interest is calculated on the accumulated amount of previous years.

Rule of 72

A quick way to estimate the time to double money at Compound Interest is T ≈ 72 ÷ Rate.
